t: How to Write a Great, Kind Email (That Is, How to Write All Emails)
q: In a caustic age of casually scathing public rhetoric, great organizational cultures are built one edifying communication at a time. It is the case that good emails accrue their cultural benefits slowly and incrementally, but bad emails can extract their cultural deficits rapidly and semi-permanently. So the skill of writing good, kind emails is an important one that directly impacts the long-term flourishing potential of our schools.

First, ask if you need to email it. Lots of times we send impulsive or lazy messages. Inboxes are places of anxiety, addiction, or both, for everybody. Those are bad. So sometimes, consider taking the extra minute or two to walk down the hall, or consider writing it on a note and letting it wait until the end of the day. At that time, you’ll be clearer on whether it really needs to be sent.

Encouraging emails are the best. Sending them (or delivering these kinds of brief, direct messages in person) trains the mind and heart to hone in on this kind of thing in others. Practice this discipline for a few years and your words will literally start to breathe life into people.

Instead, do the thinking yourself. In one group I’m involved in, we’ve resolved to only send the following kinds of emails. Notice the clear purpose behind each kind. Disciplining ourselves to these email types has led to significant improvements in both our quality of life outside of meetings and our quality of life inside of them:

Use smiley faces. A huge amount of smart people feel that emojis in emails are unprofessional. But it depends on how we view professionalism. If warmth is a part of professionalism, then generous use of the I is very professional. Tone is notoriously hard to detect in emails. So, smile.

If you become the person who mass forwards everything that’s a neat opportunity, then you’re going to train people like me to auto-archive most of your emails. Maybe create a free Mailchimp newsletter instead, ask people who are interested to “opt-in” at the next staff meeting, and then study the open and click-through rates to determine if your mass-forwarding efforts are actually reaping fruit.

Cultivate a love for people. At the end of the day, good, kind emails tend to come from good, kind people. Take a permanent diet from complaining about people, as complaining drains the soul of hope and love.
x: Bad emails damage culture fast and semi-permanently, while good ones pay off only slowly, so the skill is worth deliberate practice.
A useful default for action emails is two moves: say what you need, then communicate care.
His closing claim is that kind emails come from kind people, so the underlying work is cultivating genuine appreciation for colleagues rather than complaining about them.
Restricting a group to a few purposeful email types (proposals, weekly summaries, encouragements) improved life both inside and outside meetings.
Tone is hard to detect in text, so warmth markers such as smiley faces count as professionalism rather than detracting from it.
He recommends smiley faces for tone, restraint with mass forwarding, and acknowledging when a request is a burden.
His closing claim is that kind emails come from kind people, so the underlying work is cultivating genuine appreciation for colleagues rather than complaining about them.

q: I use this information to remind colleagues of a thing we forget: human performance is not unlimited. When people experience too much pressure — and nearly all educators do — the human soul wisely disengages. It’s either disengagement or destruction.
The heart cannot indefinitely stay emotionally connected to work that is always screaming, “MORE MORE MORE!” And so it is that only 30% of teachers tend to be engaged in their work.

The good news, of course, is that much of the pressure we feel is self-inflicted. We didn’t sign a contract at the outset that we would be the savior of our students. No — quite differently, we agreed to be professionals.
But the doctor also has enormous agency of whether or not she will become overly pressured. She gets to think about how she thinks about the work.

I used to feel that for every pop-up debate, I needed to have a rubric, and I needed to give each of my students some kind of individualized feedback. Then one day, I decided that I’d forget about those things and just listen to the students during their debate.

We identified an area for improvement today, and I taught a brief mini-lesson on that skill. And then we had another pop-up debate the same way — no rubric, no individualized feedback. Over one hundred pop-up debates later, I’ve not missed rubrics or individualized feedback a single time — and my students haven’t either.
x: Human performance is limited; unrelenting pressure leads educators to disengage or burn out.
Drawing on a Gallup finding that only about 30 percent of teachers are engaged at work, Stuart argues that the human heart disengages when pressure never lets up.

His encouraging point is that much of teachers' pressure is self-inflicted, since they agreed to be professionals rather than saviors, and he compares them to doctors who work hard for patients without being omnipotent.
Teachers have agency over how they think about their work and can act on the pressure they create.
As evidence he describes dropping rubrics and individualized feedback for pop-up debates, replacing them with listening, brief coaching, and whole-class reflection.
As evidence he describes dropping rubrics and individualized feedback for pop-up debates, replacing them with listening, brief coaching, and whole-class reflection.

q: The truth is, for the most part, it’s a sham. Expectations for student behavior in this day and age are knee-high to a five year old.

You’re asked to rely on one of the several trendy “research-based” classroom management systems your school has adopted that reject true accountability, replacing it with extrinsic rewards and appeasement.

Except for the occasional temporary improvement (e.g. students getting quiet or sitting up straight) that can happen in exchange for a reward or false praise—hence the “research”—behavior worsens over time.

All students need firmly established, nonnegotiable boundaries. If they don’t have them, in the form of clearly defined rules and their consequences, then they’ll push and probe and test until they find them.
Caring isn’t giving chance after chance. It isn’t looking the other way or excusing behavior you know is wrong. It isn’t pretending everything is okay while Rome burns.
You do right by students, and their families who have so much hope for them, by establishing boundaries that safeguard excellent teaching and inspired learning.
x: Argues that institutional talk of 'high expectations' is largely a sham as real behavior standards continue to erode.
Contends reward-based, 'research-based' classroom management systems worsen behavior over time despite occasional short-term compliance.
He argues this approach, dressed up as research-based, actually worsens behavior over time while punishing well-behaved students who quietly absorb the resulting disorder.

His counter-argument is that firm, clearly defined, consistently enforced boundaries are what make students feel safe and cared for, and that true caring means holding students accountable rather than repeatedly excusing them.
Redefines true caring as making hard, accountability-driven decisions rather than repeatedly excusing misbehavior.
Argues firm, consistently enforced boundaries make students feel safe and cared for, not oppressed.

t: A Super Easy Way To Lower Your Stress
q: It’s used by archers, golfers, surgeons, yoga teachers, and others whose performance is so directly linked to their ability to keep their composure.
The narrow passages of the nose force you to slow down your breathing, filling the lower half of your lungs and stimulating parasympathetic nerves that automatically calm the body.
It very effectively removes excitability from your classroom, which is one of the biggest causes of misbehavior. Students take their cue from you, and if you’re calm, they will be too.
Although it may take a few days to develop the habit of nasal breathing, you’ll find it delivering blessed relief within your first hour of practice.
It will show you just how profoundly a naturally calm demeanor positively influences those around you.
Your students. Your colleagues. Even the loved ones you go home to.
x: Linsin introduces nasal breathing—breathing exclusively through the nose except while talking or eating—as a simple, scientifically grounded technique for staying calm throughout the teaching day.
Explains that narrow nasal passages naturally slow breathing and engage the parasympathetic nervous system.

He also connects the practice to classroom management directly, noting that it discourages excessive narrating, reminding, and micromanaging of students, and that a calm teacher visibly transmits calm to the class.
Claims noticeable relief can occur within the very first hour of practicing the technique.

t: On Sunk Costs (and Whether You Should Change Your Curriculum Even When You Recently Spent a Lot of Money on the Current One) hen-you-recently-spent-a-lot-of-money-on-the-current-one/
q: The X dollars is a sunk cost — money you can’t recover, whether you stick with the curriculum for ten more years or you abandon it tomorrow. When we continue a behavior just because we spent unrecoverable money on the behavior in the past, we engage in the sunk cost fallacy. We’re susceptible to this in all parts of life, but it’s uniquely deadly when we do it with curriculum decisions because of how many people it adversely affects.

If the answer is no, then make prudent haste in pursuing the new and better curricula. And that word prudent should be size 48 font — I mean it! This time, rethink your due diligence, e.g., don’t open-invite people to the curriculum committee.

Don’t ask for the opinions of all stakeholders — we’re in the education profession, not the please-everybody one. Consult the research, consult the case studies, consult the experts who have no money to gain from your decision but who have a reputation for helping you make a good one.
And for goodness sake, consider options that don’t cost X dollars! There are many good ones that cost a fraction of X.

Before you do any more curricula adoption, your team should read The Knowledge Gap by Natalie Wexler. Wexler provides an intelligible, robust overview of the things you need to know in order to make your next curriculum decision a good one, including:
x: Money already spent on a curriculum is irrecoverable and should not decide whether to keep it.
He lists what a bad curriculum can look like, from being superseded by better research to having incoherent vertical gaps.

He urges prudence in the replacement process, with a small committee that consults research, case studies, and disinterested experts rather than polling every stakeholder, and a willingness to consider cheaper options.
Stuart argues that a district should not keep a bad curriculum simply because it recently spent money on it, since that money is a sunk cost whichever way the decision goes.
He closes by recommending Natalie Wexler's The Knowledge Gap as required reading before the next adoption.

t: The Four Pillars of High School Success
q: Every year of a child’s education is important, but ninth grade performance is especially predictive of graduation outcomes. One reason for this is that even though the five key beliefs beneath student motivation are always malleable, they are especially so at times of transition.

Critically, all four of the teachers on the team speak to the students about these pillars as we see fit in our classes. This means four academic environments — science, math, English, and history — where the same messaging about holistic high school success is communicated.

On academic success days, we pull GPA data for all students and divvy up interventions for any students with a 2.5 GPA or lower. The intervention is so simple it’s dumb: a moment of genuine connection plus an invitation to what we call Monday Academic Center (MAC), the one afternoon per week when all four of us teachers are available to help students in a relaxed study hall environment.
And from a “manage the pressure” standpoint, these meetings don’t produce laborious work. We just take 30 seconds or so in the next week to check in with a quarter of our students who are struggling.

When we see students who aren’t involved in anything, we put them on the intervention list. Guess what the intervention is? A moment of genuine connection and an encouragement to try out a club or sport or activity that aligns with their interests.
On plan for the future days, we coordinate a series of guest speakers with diverse post-high-school paths. Each of us is responsible for bringing in two guests per semester.
x: He grounds the focus on ninth grade in the fact that performance that year predicts graduation outcomes and that student motivation beliefs are especially malleable at transitions.
The four teachers across science, math, English, and history deliver the same message to students, which gives an otherwise fragmented school day some coherence.
Interventions are intentionally tiny, a brief personal connection plus an invitation to a club, sport, or weekly help session, so the work stays sustainable.
Each weekly meeting targets a single pillar, which keeps the team focused rather than scattered.
A weekly 45-minute meeting rotates through the pillars, each with a deliberately light intervention built on a moment of genuine connection.

Dave Stuart Jr. describes how his school's ninth-grade transition team organizes its work around four shared pillars: academic success, social success, a plan for the future, and enjoying the process.

t: How To Respond After Losing Your Cool
q: You’re convinced that you’ve ruined everything, that you’ve undone all the influence, trust, and goodwill you’ve built up since the start of the year.
Although you may wince, it’s helpful to understand why you reacted the way you did. This alone goes a long way toward ensuring that it doesn’t happen again.
I messed up. It wasn’t okay how I reacted. It wasn’t okay that I didn’t follow through on my promise to protect your right to learn and enjoy being part of this class.
Second, students—and people in general—are quick to forgive those who openly admit their wrongdoings. It’s rare in this day and age, and thus more powerful and meaningful than ever.
Third, vulnerability makes you more likable. It makes you more authentic and your lessons more interesting, allowing you to build easy rapport with your students.
It will make you more confident and influential. It will make you more of the kind of leader your students will respect and admire.
x: Linsin offers a structured recovery process for teachers who lose their composure and react emotionally instead of following their classroom management plan.
Linsin offers a structured recovery process for teachers who lose their composure and react emotionally instead of following their classroom management plan.
Linsin offers a structured recovery process for teachers who lose their composure and react emotionally instead of following their classroom management plan.
Argues that openly owning a mistake models accountability for students rather than signaling weakness.
Claims vulnerability from a teacher makes them more likable and easier to build rapport with, not less authoritative.

t: How To Give Effective Praise: 6 Guidelines
q: Typically, praise is given far too frequently. Most classrooms are a constant stream of way-to-gos and good-jobs, regardless of accomplishment—or lack thereof.
It’s also often used dishonestly as a tool to manipulate students into desired behavior.
Praise should be directed not at the student(s) themselves—as in, “You’re an amazing writer!”—but at their accomplishment.
Praise that inspires students to greater levels of achievement is honest, specific, authentic (often subtle), and based not on natural ability, but on the process of learning, growing, and maturing.
It’s perfectly okay to let them wallow in their success without your input.

It supports a growth mindset. It drives students toward mastery and the profound intrinsic rewards of learning and acquiring skill, knowledge, and the confidence to tackle more and greater challenges with gusto.
x: Recommends directing praise at accomplishments rather than at the student's identity or innate ability.
Linsin, who says he's written about praise since 2009, warns against both overusing false, indiscriminate praise and swinging too far toward withholding it altogether.
